title: Wine, Weights, and the Lamp of the LORD
summary: The chapter opens with wine as a mocker and moves through a wide range of daily matters: the king's terror and justice, the slacker who does not plow, the hidden purposes of the heart, haggling buyers, collateral for loans, rash vows, and differing weights that the LORD detests. At its heart are sayings that humble every reader: no one can claim a pure heart, a person's steps are from the LORD, and the human spirit is the lamp of the LORD searching the inmost being.
story: The Solomonic collection is moving toward its close at 22:16, and chapter 20 gathers many of its earlier themes into one place: the king, honest trade, laziness, speech, and the LORD's oversight of human life. What is newer is a sustained note of humility about self-knowledge. The heart's intentions are deep waters (verse 5), no one can say he has kept his heart pure (verse 9), and no one fully understands his own way (verse 24). The wise person of this chapter is not the one who has mastered himself but the one who knows how much of himself he cannot see and entrusts it to God.
historical:
Four sayings concern the king (verses 2, 8, 26, and 28). In Israel the king was the highest court of appeal. He sat on a throne of judgment and was expected to sort out evil from good, as Solomon did in the case of the two women and the child (1 Kings 3:16-28). Verse 26 pictures the king separating out the wicked the way a farmer separates grain from chaff, driving the threshing wheel over them. Verse 28 names what actually preserves a throne: not force but loving devotion and faithfulness, the covenant virtues God himself shows. Israel's history, with its many kings who fell to conspiracy and violence, gave this saying weight.

Verse 25 warns against rash vows. Israelites could vow gifts or service to the LORD, and the law required that a vow once made be kept (Deuteronomy 23:21-23; Numbers 30:2). Ecclesiastes gives the same warning, advising that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). The story of Jephthah (Judges 11:30-40) shows how disastrous a hasty vow could be.
cultural:
Verse 1 names wine and strong drink. Wine was a normal part of Israelite life and a sign of God's blessing (Psalm 104:15), and strong drink (shekar) probably refers to beer or other fermented beverages. Proverbs does not forbid either, but it warns vividly that they mock and brawl, and that whoever is led astray by them is not wise. A fuller warning comes in 23:29-35.

Verse 14 is a scene from the market. The buyer runs down the goods, saying they are worthless, to lower the price, then walks away boasting of his bargain. Verse 16 concerns collateral. A lender could take a garment as a pledge, but the law required that a poor man's cloak be returned by sunset because it was his only covering at night (Exodus 22:26-27). The saying advises taking the garment of someone rash enough to guarantee a stranger's debt, since such a person is a poor risk. Verse 26's threshing wheel refers to the heavy wheels of a cart or sledge driven over harvested grain to break the husks, a technique also mentioned in Isaiah 28:27-28.
literary: This chapter mixes many forms: rhetorical questions (verses 6, 9, 24), commands (verses 13, 16, 18, 19, 22), a quoted speech (verse 14), and several sayings that name the LORD directly (verses 10, 12, 22, 23, 24, 27). Two sayings on differing weights (verses 10 and 23) frame a section of the chapter and echo 11:1 and 16:11. Verses 5 and 27 both speak of the inner depths of a person, the first as deep waters a man of understanding can draw out and the second as the inmost being that the LORD's lamp searches. The chapter closes with contrasting pairs: young and old (verse 29), and the painful discipline that cleanses (verse 30).

outline.t: Wine, the king's anger, quarrels, and the slacker
Deep purposes, faithful men, a just king, and no pure heart
Differing weights, known by actions, and the buyer's boast
Collateral, fraud, counsel, gossip, and cursing parents
Wait on the LORD; steps from the LORD; rash vows
The king's justice, the lamp of the LORD, and cleansing discipline

doctrines.note: Verse 9 asks who can claim to have kept his heart pure, expecting the answer no one. Proverbs, which speaks constantly of the righteous, still recognizes that sin runs through every human heart, a truth stated elsewhere in 1 Kings 8:46 and Ecclesiastes 7:20.
A man's steps are from the LORD, so how can anyone understand his own way (verse 24)? The saying humbles human planning without denying human responsibility, and it invites trust rather than anxiety.

Do not avenge evil; wait on the LORD, and he will save (verse 22). Judgment belongs to God, and the wise refuse to take it into their own hands. The same God detests dishonest weights (verses 10, 23) and will set things right.

words.note: Qavah, to wait for or hope in. The verb has the sense of eager, expectant waiting, looking toward someone who will act. It is the verb in Isaiah 40:31, those who wait upon the LORD. In verse 22 it is the alternative to vengeance: instead of repaying evil, the wise person waits for the LORD to deliver.

Ner, lamp. Verse 20 uses it for the life of one who curses his parents, which will be snuffed out in deep darkness. Verse 27 makes the human spirit (literally breath) the lamp of the LORD, searching the inmost parts. Interpreters debate whether this means that God searches a person by means of the spirit he gave, or that conscience is a light God has placed within. Either way, nothing inside is hidden.

Zakah, to be clean or pure. Verse 9 uses it in a rhetorical question: who can say he has made his heart clean? The same verb appears in Psalm 73:13, where the psalmist wonders whether he kept his heart pure in vain. Moral cleanness is something people long for and cannot finally produce in themselves.

christ: Verse 9's question, who can say his heart is pure, stands behind the New Testament's insistence that all have sinned (Romans 3:23) and that if we claim to be without sin we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). Proverbs asks the question; the gospel answers it by pointing to the one who cleanses from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Verse 22's call to wait on the LORD rather than avenge evil is taken up by Paul, who tells believers never to take revenge but to leave room for God's wrath (Romans 12:17-19), and it is lived out by Jesus, who did not retaliate but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Verse 28's king preserved by loving devotion and faithfulness describes the kind of ruler Israel longed for and the New Testament finds in Christ, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). These are thematic links that follow the direction the proverbs themselves point.

hard.q: If no one can say his heart is pure (verse 9), who are the righteous that Proverbs keeps praising?
hard.a:
Proverbs uses righteous in two ways that can seem to clash. It constantly contrasts the righteous with the wicked as two kinds of people, and yet verse 9 implies that no one is morally spotless. The tension is real, but it is not a contradiction. In the Old Testament the righteous person is not a sinless person but one whose life is oriented toward God and his ways: who fears the LORD, deals honestly, confesses sin, and turns from evil. David, called a man after God's own heart, is also the author of Psalm 51. Righteousness in this sense is a direction of life, not a perfect record.

Christian theology adds a further layer. The New Testament teaches that no one is righteous by his own performance (Romans 3:10) and that righteousness before God is received as a gift through faith in Christ. Those who are declared righteous in this way are then called to live righteously, which is where the practical wisdom of Proverbs comes in. Different traditions describe the relation between the gift and the life in different terms, but all agree that verse 9 rules out self-righteousness and that the righteous of Proverbs are people who know they need mercy.

questions: Verse 5 says a person's purposes are deep waters. Who in your life is good at drawing out what is really going on inside you?
Verse 22 says not to avenge evil but to wait on the LORD. What wrong are you tempted to repay, and what would waiting look like?
Verse 9 asks who can say his heart is pure. How does admitting you cannot say it change the way you treat others who fail?
